column4: The ayah says no action or state is absent from Allah, down to an atom's weight, and that it is recorded; this extends the section's unseen-observer claim to every deed and its record.
People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and reveal; this directly stages the hiddenness the section's man presumes.
The ayah equates one who hides a statement with one who declares it, and the person hidden by night with the one abroad by day; it directly dissolves the public/private boundary in the section.
People are told to act because Allah, His Messenger, and the believers will see their deeds; this makes the section's unseen action explicitly visible and answerable.
The command to “watch for” the coming day uses ارتقب from the source-section root ر ق ب, in the section's sense of watching and awaiting what is coming.
Allah does not disclose His unseen to أَحَدًا, “anyone”; this meets the section's link between أَحَدٌ (“anyone”) and عين (“eye”) in a verse about who may know what is hidden.
The next ayah makes an exception for a chosen messenger and places guards before and behind him; it completes 72:26 with both disclosure and watchfulness.
Each person's deed is fastened to his neck, then brought out as an open record; this joins the section's neck and watcher details in one bodily image of unavoidable accounting.
The person is told to read his book and finds himself sufficient as his own accountant; it completes 17:13 by showing what the neck-borne record requires.
The opened book omits neither small nor great deeds, and people see what they did present before them; this gives the section's claim of unwitnessed acts an exhaustive record scene.
On the Day of Judgment, people's tongues, hands, and feet testify to what they did; this repeats the section's image of bodily faculties becoming witnesses against their owner.
The mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people earned; it repeats the bodily testimony scene with a different set of organs.
The ayah says a person's striving will be seen, سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ; it directly joins the section's sight motif to deeds and their recompense.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ; this makes the section's unseen watcher an explicit companion at judgment.
A person with abundant provision says his Lord has honored him; this parallels the section's wealthy man's assumption that material spending proves his security.
The ayah says people love wealth intensely; this sharpens the parallel to the man who boasts of spending heaps of money while leaving the needy uncared for.

The passage describes the person who considers himself self-sufficient, وَأَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ; this is a close parallel to the section's wealthy man who imagines himself beyond anyone's power or sight.

The following scene turns to a blind man who comes seeking guidance; unlike the affluent self-satisfied person, he is the one asking for attention, paralleling the section's care for the poor and its limits of sight.
The needy who refrain from asking are recognized by their mark, بِسِيمَاهُمْ; this meets the section's image of a person as a visible sign and its mention of the destitute covered in dust.
The wealth-counter thinks his wealth will make him last forever; this exposes the self-security behind the counting that the section connects to the question and fire.

Clear proofs have come, and whoever sees benefits himself while whoever is blind harms himself; the verse joins visible signs, moral blindness, and the limit of a guardian, all developed in the section.
The ayah says Allah encompasses what the messengers have and counts everything; it completes 72:26–27 by confirming the disclosure and the full accounting around it.
This ayah identifies the speaker in 69:26 as the one given his book in his left hand; it is the needed context for the section's quotation of his words.
The speaker says he will cast the man into Saqar; it frames the “what is Saqar?” question in 74:27 that the section cites as a fire-opening formula.
The ayah says the wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher; it introduces the question at 104:5 and its fire-answer in 104:6.
Nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from Allah; this supplies a concise boundary to the man's belief that no one saw him.
Allah knows every leaf that falls and every grain, wet or dry, recorded in a clear book; this gives the section's unseen-observer claim a concrete image of nothing escaping notice.
Whether people conceal or declare their speech, Allah knows what is within their breasts; it directly joins hidden words to inward knowledge.
What people disclose or conceal within themselves is still brought to account by Allah; it makes inner hiddenness answerable, as in the section's image.
Linked to 13:10, successive guardians preserve each person by Allah's command; it supplies the watcher behind the ayah's contrast of hidden and public conduct.
The ayah closes with Allah as رَقِيبًا over all things, repeating the source-section root ر ق ب in its watchful-guardian sense.
The awaited smoke covers people and is a painful torment; it completes 44:10 by showing what the root ر ق ب commands the hearer to watch for.
The closing command “watch; they too are watching” repeats the source-section root ر ق ب as waiting for an outcome.
The command وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا forbids spying on one another; it gives the section's secondary image of an eye sent to gather news a human setting and a moral boundary.

The example contrasts an owned slave unable to act with a person given good provision who spends openly and secretly; it joins the section's freed neck, hidden conduct, and boast about wealth in one comparison.
The self remains witness even if it offers excuses; it completes 75:14 by showing that self-testimony cannot be evaded.
The next ayah says Allah will pay them their true recompense; it completes 24:24 by linking bodily testimony to judgment.
The day when hidden matters are exposed, تَبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ, gives a direct counterpart to the section's insistence that what seems unseen will become known.
Allah teaches the human what he did not know; this gives the section's point about what cannot be known without disclosure a concrete parallel.
The addressee attends to the self-sufficient man; it completes 80:5 and sharpens the contrast with the blind seeker who follows.
The blind visitor comes with concern and fear; it completes 80:8 by showing his earnest stance, which makes the turning-away in 80:10 consequential.
The addressee is distracted from the blind seeker; it completes the scene begun in 80:8 and contrasts with the section's call to feed and aid those in need.
The believers' mark is visible on their faces; this is a bodily identifier parallel to the section's secondary āya sense of a person's visible form.
The written records are spread open; this is a specific afterlife scene of deeds becoming visible, fitting the section's account of unwitnessed acts.
Whether people disclose what is within themselves or conceal it, Allah knows it; this is another direct boundary on the privacy imagined in the section.

Those who deny the signs are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this parallels the section's secondary d-r-y image of a hunter approaching prey unseen, though the verse itself describes divine enticement rather than hunting.
The next ayah says the deniers are given respite and that God's plan is firm; it completes the gradual, unperceived approach in 7:182.
Those who deny the Reminder are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this repeats the specific unseen-approach image in 7:182 and the section's hunter/prey lexical image.
The next ayah grants them respite; it completes the unseen gradual drawing in 68:44.
People are brought forward with no hidden thing of theirs concealed; this states the opposite of the left-hand man's imagined privacy and leads into the book scenes.
The person given his book in his right hand says to read it; this supplies the opposite book-receiving outcome to 69:25–26, which the section cites.
He says he knew he would meet his account; it completes 69:19 and contrasts with the left-hand speaker's not knowing his account in 69:26.
The record speaks truth and states that what people did was being written; this repeats the section's image of actions made present as testimony.
The person interprets reduced provision as humiliation; the surah immediately corrects that judgment by pointing to neglect of the orphan and poor, reversing wealth as a measure of worth.
The condemned are asked what brought them into Saqar; it introduces the punishment whose answer in 74:44 includes failure to feed the poor.
The orphan is not to be oppressed; this reverses the neglect of vulnerable people that the section contrasts with mercy.
The person who asks is not to be repelled; this reverses the section's call to feed and aid the needy.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned; this is a boundary opposite to the section's freeing of a neck.
The next ayah excepts the people of the right; it completes 74:38 with the divided outcome echoed by the section's companions of the right and left.
Heavy scales bring a good life, the explicit reverse of the light scales and fire the section names.
The pleasant life completes the heavy-scale side of the contrast with the light-scaled person in 101:8–11.
The ayah says it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts in the breasts; this sets a boundary between the section's sensory eye and inward recognition.
The blind and seeing are not equal, nor are believers who do good and the evildoer; this explicitly joins perception with the moral distinction made in the section.
The disbelievers' hearing is sealed and a covering is over their sight; this repeats the section's contrast between eyes given and eyes unable or unwilling to perceive.
The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing, or darkness and light, are equal; it uses sight as a measure of recognition, directly matching the section's eye-and-guidance link.
The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing are equal; this is another direct Qur'anic formulation of the perception boundary developed in the section.
The blind and the seeing are declared unequal; this repeats the section's physical and moral sight contrast in a brief direct formulation.
Some look toward the Prophet, but he cannot guide the blind who do not see; the verse distinguishes looking from true perception as the section does.
